Serbia. This Balkan nation in southeastern Europe played a pivotal role in the outbreak of World War I. After centuries of Ottoman domination, Serbia regained independence in the nineteenth century and emerged as a focal point of South Slavic nationalism. Pan-Slavic nationalism made Serbia a champion of Balkan independence and a rival to Austria-Hungary's multinational empire. In 1914, a terrorist organization known as the Black Hand, composed of Serbian nationalists and military officers, coordinated the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia for the assassination and issued a harsh ultimatum. When Serbia rejected this ultimatum, it triggered the alliance system that caused World War I. Russia supported Serbia, viewing it as a Slavic ally and a check on Austro-Hungarian expansion, which deepened great power tensions. Serbia's rejection of Austria-Hungary's ultimatum drew in Russia, which mobilized to defend the Serbs, and this in turn brought France and Germany into the conflict. The consequence of this diplomatic crisis was the outbreak of war that would reshape the European map. After World War I, Serbia expanded to become the core of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, which was later renamed Yugoslavia. Serbia's position in the great power tensions of early twentieth-century Europe made it the focal point of the very crisis that ignited the First World War.
